prompt.context: Your client serves the paper industry with specialty chemicals. The company currently operates just above breakeven. It serves 250 accounts with a sales force of 150 'sales and service engineers' throughout Asia. Industry growth is moderate at 3–6% depending on paper industry utilization rates. The client is the weak #5 player in a market dominated by 6 players, with some limited fragmentation. The top 6 players compete on service, product technology, and tailored 'solutions'.
prompt.question: How would you approach this problem of improving the client's profitability?

clarifying_info.q: What are the switching costs or barriers at the account level?
clarifying_info.a: Switching barriers are high at the account level, largely driven by 'papermaking' chemistry.

clarifying_info.q: How variable is profitability across accounts?
clarifying_info.a: Account profitability varies wildly by size, type, and penetration.

clarifying_info.q: What are the product margins like?
clarifying_info.a: Product margins are high and highly variable, ranging from approximately 20% to 60%.

clarifying_info.q: What do industry leaders achieve in terms of profitability?
clarifying_info.a: Industry leaders enjoy 15–18% return on sales (ROS).

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost and capital structure of the business?
clarifying_info.a: Very low fixed cost and capital are required; barriers to entry are account-level share/relationships and product technology.

framework: Construct a simple P&L to understand cost structure — identify that the sales force is the dominant cost (60%+ of total costs)
Recognize the very local nature of the business (single mill site focus)
Identify accounts as the scarce resource to be optimized, focusing on profit per account
Probe account-level economics to separate 'good' accounts from 'poor' ones
Assess how to improve (not simply cut) unprofitable accounts

questions.prompt: What does a simple P&L reveal about the cost structure?
questions.guidance: The sales force ('sales and service engineers') represents 60%+ of total costs. This makes account-level productivity and cost-to-serve the key profitability driver. The candidate should recognize this before diving into revenue levers.

A good account has: (1) sufficient size to generate meaningful revenue, (2) high-quality revenue mix tilted toward high-margin products (top of the 20–60% margin range), and (3) manageable cost-to-serve (e.g., fewer on-site staff required). Account share is crucial — it typically takes at least one full-time person to serve an account even at low share, so the business has a semi-fixed cost nature. High share dramatically improves profitability per account.

questions.prompt: How can the client improve profitability on weak or small accounts rather than simply exiting them?
questions.guidance: Outstanding candidates will go beyond 'cut unprofitable accounts' to identify improvement levers: (1) Ownership of critical applications builds trust and drives follow-on sales, leading to high account share. (2) Individual skills and performance of the sales/service engineer make a large difference in relationships, service quality, solution tailoring, and local marketing/selling. (3) A low cost-to-serve, low margin/revenue model could be designed specifically for small accounts to make them profitable rather than eliminating them.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers can the client use to improve profitability across its account portfolio?

categories.name: Revenue quality
ideas: Shift product mix toward higher-margin specialty chemicals (20–60% margin range)
Focus selling effort on applications where the client has technological differentiation
Capture follow-on sales by owning critical papermaking applications first

categories.name: Account share
ideas: Increase share of wallet at existing accounts to spread fixed cost-to-serve
Target accounts where competitors have low share or poor service relationships
Leverage high switching barriers once a critical application is owned

categories.name: Cost-to-serve management
ideas: Right-size on-site staffing per account based on revenue and margin potential
Create a tiered service model: high-touch for large/high-margin accounts, low-cost for small accounts
Improve sales engineer productivity through better territory design

categories.name: Account portfolio optimization
ideas: Rank all 250 accounts by profit contribution (revenue × margin – cost-to-serve)
Identify accounts to grow, hold, restructure, or exit
Design a low-cost coverage model (e.g., remote/digital) for marginal small accounts instead of simply dropping them

categories.name: People and capabilities
ideas: Hire or develop sales engineers with strong technical chemistry skills to improve solution tailoring
Incentivize engineers on account profitability, not just revenue
Share best practices from top-performing engineers across the 150-person sales force

recommendation: Prioritize increasing account share at the most profitable large accounts, as the semi-fixed cost structure means incremental revenue at existing accounts flows almost entirely to the bottom line
Restructure coverage of small accounts using a lower-cost service model to avoid outright exits while eliminating unprofitable cost-to-serve
Focus product mix efforts on high-margin specialty applications where the client can own a critical step in the papermaking process, creating loyalty and follow-on revenue
risks: Aggressive cost-to-serve reductions at small accounts may damage relationships and trigger exits to competitors
The client's weak #5 position means it lacks scale advantages enjoyed by leaders; improvement may be incremental unless a step-change in account share is achieved
Talent dependency is high — individual engineer skill is a key driver, so attrition in the sales force is a material risk
next_steps: Conduct a full account-level P&L analysis across all 250 accounts to quantify the profit distribution
Benchmark the top 10–15 most profitable accounts to identify what 'good' looks like and replicate it
Pilot a low-cost service model for the bottom quartile of accounts and measure impact on retention and profitability
